lessons.title: Small Loans, Big Idea: The Birth of Microfinance
lessons.content:
## A Working Definition

**Microfinance** means providing basic financial services small loans, savings accounts, insurance, and payment services to people who are shut out of the traditional banking system. The best-known piece is **microcredit**: very small loans given to low-income entrepreneurs to start or grow tiny businesses, like a food stall, a tailor shop, or a goat-rearing operation.

The idea rests on a simple observation: poor people are not poor because they lack skills or work ethic. Often they lack only **access** to capital, to a safe place to save, to a way to smooth out a bad month.

## The Jobra Experiment, 1976

The modern microfinance movement traces back to one village and one economics professor. In 1974, a famine struck Bangladesh. **Muhammad Yunus**, who taught economics at Chittagong University, found that his elegant classroom theories felt hollow while people starved outside. He began visiting the neighboring village of **Jobra** to understand poverty up close.

There he met craftswomen who made bamboo stools. They worked hard all day but earned almost nothing, because they had to borrow from traders to buy raw bamboo and the traders demanded they sell the finished stools back to them at prices the traders set. The women were trapped: too poor to buy materials, too indebted to keep their profits.

In 1976, Yunus did something radical in its simplicity. He lent **about $27 of his own money to 42 villagers** so they could buy materials and work for themselves. Every borrower repaid. Conventional banks, he noticed, would never have made those loans they demanded collateral, paperwork, and loan sizes far bigger than a stool maker needed.

## From Experiment to Grameen Bank

Yunus spent years persuading banks to lend to the poor, offering himself as guarantor. When that proved too slow, he created a bank for the poor instead. **Grameen Bank** "gram" means "village" in Bengali was formally established in 1983. Its model flipped banking upside down:

- Lend to the **poorest**, especially women
- Require **no collateral**
- Organize borrowers into small **groups**
- Collect repayment in tiny, frequent **installments**

Grameen grew to serve millions of borrowers, and in **2006, Yunus and Grameen Bank were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize** for showing that credit could be a tool against poverty.

## More Than Loans

Today "microfinance" covers a family of services:

- **Microcredit** small business and emergency loans
- **Microsavings** safe deposit accounts with tiny minimums
- **Microinsurance** health, crop, and life cover for a few cents a week
- **Payments and transfers** often delivered by mobile phone

> "The poor themselves can create a poverty-free world all we have to do is to free them from the chains that we have put around them." Muhammad Yunus

Consider **Fatima**, who borrows $200 to buy a used sewing machine. She stitches clothes for her neighbors, repays a few dollars each week, and within a year owns the machine outright. That is microfinance at work: not charity, but access.

lessons.title: Financial Inclusion: Who Microfinance Serves and Why
lessons.content:
## The Unbanked World

Around the world, roughly **1.4 billion adults have no account at a bank or other financial institution**, according to the World Bank's Global Findex survey. Being **unbanked** does not mean having no money it means having nowhere safe to keep it, no way to borrow formally, and no record to build on. The unbanked save in cash at home, borrow from moneylenders, and rely on relatives in emergencies.

**Financial inclusion** is the effort to bring these households into the formal financial system with services that fit their lives: tiny deposits, small loans, and payments that work without a payslip or a permanent address.

## Why Traditional Banks Stayed Away

Banks did not ignore the poor out of pure prejudice; the economics pushed them away:

- **No collateral.** A landless farmer has no titled property to pledge against a loan.
- **No credit history.** Informal workers leave no paper trail a bank can score.
- **Tiny transactions.** A $150 loan costs nearly as much paperwork as a $150,000 one, but earns a fraction of the revenue.
- **Distance.** Serving scattered rural villages means travel, staff, and cash handling that eat up thin margins.
- **Irregular income.** A harvest arrives twice a year; daily wages fluctuate. Standard monthly loan schedules fit poorly.
- **Paperwork barriers.** Forms, identity documents, and literacy requirements screen many people out before a loan is even discussed.

The result: a vegetable seller with a thriving stall could not borrow $100 from a bank, but a moneylender would happily lend it at rates that swallowed her profit.

## Who Microfinance Serves

Microfinance institutions (MFIs) designed their model around exactly the clients banks rejected:

- **Women**, who make up the large majority of microfinance clients worldwide in part because banks excluded them the most, and because early experience suggested they invested earnings heavily in their children's food and schooling
- **Market vendors and stallholders** needing small amounts of working capital
- **Smallholder farmers** buying seed and fertilizer before the planting season
- **Artisans and home-based workers** weavers, potters, food processors
- **Informal laborers** smoothing income between jobs

Consider **Rosa**, who sells fruit in a town market. Each morning she needs $30 of stock. Without microfinance, a wholesaler lends her the money at 10% *per day*. With a microloan at a fraction of that cost, she keeps her margin and starts saving for the first time.

## The Promise and the Honest Caveats

Microfinance has reached **hundreds of millions of clients** globally, and studies suggest it helps many households smooth consumption, keep children in school during lean months, and grow micro-businesses. But researchers also urge honesty: microcredit is **not a magic exit from poverty** for everyone. Loans used for emergencies rather than business can leave families deeper in debt, and some borrowers juggle multiple loans at once. Later modules look at savings, insurance, and consumer protection the pieces that make the toolkit safer.

> Access to finance is a tool, not a cure: it amplifies whatever a household already does with money.

modules.title: Microcredit I: How Small Loans Work

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Microloan
lessons.content:
## Small by Design

A **microloan** is built for a business that fits in a market stall. While sizes vary by country and lender, typical first loans often fall in the range of **$50 to $500** enough for a sewing machine, a bicycle rickshaw, or a crate of goods to resell. Terms are short, commonly **three to twelve months**, and repayment happens in tiny, frequent installments often **weekly**.

This design is deliberate. A weekly installment of a few dollars matches the daily cash flow of a vendor who earns a little every day. It also surfaces trouble early: if a borrower misses week two, the lender knows long before a year-long loan would have quietly gone bad.

## The Solidarity Group

The signature invention of early microcredit was **group lending**. In the Grameen-style model, borrowers form **self-selected groups of about five people** neighbors, friends, market colleagues. Each member receives her own loan for her own business, but the group takes responsibility together.

Why groups instead of individuals?

- **Screening.** Members know each other's reputations. A group rarely accepts someone it considers unreliable, because the group will pay the price.
- **Monitoring.** Between lender visits, members keep an eye on whether loans are used as promised.
- **Support.** Members share advice, cover small gaps, and encourage one another through slow weeks.
- **Lower cost.** One loan officer can serve five borrowers in a single meeting, which keeps the lender's costs down.

A typical sequence: the group forms, members receive basic financial training, the first two members get loans and begin repayment, and the rest follow once the first two show discipline. Lending in stages builds a track record inside the group itself.

## A Week in the Life

Picture **Amina**, a vegetable seller in a five-woman group. She borrows $120 for wholesale stock. Every Friday morning the group meets the loan officer under a tree; Amina hands over about $10 principal plus interest. The officer records the payment in each member's passbook. The meeting takes an hour, and members also swap news: whose daughter is sick, whose supplier cheated them, who found a cheaper wholesaler.

## What the Loan Actually Buys

Most microloans fund **working capital** stock, raw materials, seeds rather than big equipment. The business earns a margin on fast turnover: buy vegetables at dawn, sell out by noon, repay a slice on Friday, repeat. When the cycle works, each loan round leaves the borrower slightly better stocked than the last.

Groups typically graduate to **larger loans over successive cycles** as trust and repayment history build. That is why a first loan is often small even when a borrower's plans are big: the small loan is the entrance exam, and repayment is the passing grade.

lessons.title: Trust as Collateral: Joint Liability and Character-Based Lending
lessons.content:
## Lending Without Collateral

Traditional loans rest on **collateral** property the bank can seize if you default. Microcredit's clients have none, so the model substitutes something else: **social trust**, made concrete through two tools **joint liability** and **character-based underwriting**.

## Joint Liability

In a group loan, members are **jointly liable**: if one member cannot pay, the others must cover her installment, or the whole group loses access to future loans. This sounds harsh, but it converts a borrower's strongest asset her standing among neighbors into loan security.

- Members choose groupmates carefully, because a careless choice becomes their own problem.
- Members help each other in a crunch, because one default endangers everyone's credit line.
- Lenders can skip expensive collateral checks, because the group performs them socially.

## Character-Based Underwriting

With no credit scores and no collateral, how does a lender decide who gets a loan? By reading **character and cash flow** instead of paperwork:

- **Reputation.** The group itself vouches for members; local standing substitutes for a credit bureau file.
- **Business visits.** A loan officer walks the borrower's stall or workshop, counts stock, and asks about daily sales and costs.
- **Cash-flow logic.** The question is not "what do you own?" but "does this business bring in enough each week to cover the installment?"
- **Progressive lending.** Borrowers prove themselves with a small loan, then qualify for larger ones repayment history becomes the borrower's credit record.

## The Weekly Meeting

Repayment usually happens at a **group meeting**, held weekly or every two weeks, often in a public spot in the village. Meetings do several jobs at once:

- Collect installments transparently everyone sees who paid, recorded in passbooks
- Create **repayment discipline**: a fixed, frequent, public appointment is hard to forget
- Deliver training on budgeting, health, or business skills
- Let the loan officer spot problems early a member who starts arriving late, or borrowing from neighbors to pay, is signaling trouble

## The Honest Risks

Group lending's strengths can cut both ways. **Peer pressure** can slide from encouragement into coercion; there are documented cases of groups seizing a defaulting member's assets, and of women borrowing from moneylenders just to keep up appearances at meetings. A single local shock a flood, an illness outbreak can knock out several members of one group at once, because neighbors often share the same local economy.

Well-run lenders therefore pair joint liability with flexibility: rescheduling for genuine hardship, keeping loan sizes modest, and never treating the group's pressure as a substitute for humane judgment. Used well, trust-based lending achieves repayment rates that conventional bankers once insisted were impossible among the poor. Used badly, it can turn a neighborly safety net into a trap.

lessons.title: Lending Models: From Solidarity Groups to Village Banks
lessons.content:
## One Size Does Not Fit All

Microcredit is not a single product. Over the decades, practitioners developed several **lending models**, each suited to different clients and communities. The three you will meet most often are **solidarity group lending**, **individual lending**, and **village banking**.

## Solidarity Group Lending (Recap)

The previous module covered this model: self-selected groups of about five, joint liability, weekly meetings. It works best for first-time borrowers with tiny working-capital needs and strong local ties. Its weakness: loan sizes stay small, and group pressure is not for everyone.

## Individual Lending

As businesses grow, many borrowers "graduate" to **individual microloans**:

- **Larger amounts** from a few hundred to several thousand dollars
- **One borrower, one contract** no group liability
- **Some security** a guarantor, business assets, or a co-signer may replace group pressure
- **Longer terms** a year or more, matching bigger investments like equipment or a shop lease

Individual lending suits established micro-enterprises with steady records. The lender underwrites the business itself visiting the shop, reviewing sales, checking references much as the group once did socially. Many MFIs run both models side by side: groups as the entry ramp, individual loans as the highway.

## Village Banking

A **village bank** is bigger and more community-run than a solidarity group. Typically **20 to 30 members** often women form a single association that:

1. Receives one **external loan** from a microfinance institution
2. Re-lends that money to members as small internal loans
3. Collects **member savings** into an "internal account," which members can also borrow from
4. Manages its own records, sets internal loan terms, and enforces repayment itself

The MFI relates to the village bank as a wholesale lender; the village bank is the retail shop, run by the community. Because members' own savings circulate inside the bank, members earn returns on their deposits and the institution's capital goes further. When the external loan is repaid, the cycle repeats often with members' growing savings providing more and more of the funds.

Picture **twenty-five women in a lakeside village**. Their village bank borrows $1,250 from an MFI and re-lends it as $50 internal loans for stock and seed. Members also deposit a dollar or two of savings each week. By the third annual cycle, their own savings fund most of the lending and the MFI's money has become a boost, not a lifeline.

## Related Models Worth Knowing

- **Self-help groups (SHGs)** especially widespread in **India**; small groups that save together first, then lend internally, and later link up with banks
- **Credit unions and cooperatives** member-owned institutions that pool savings and lend to members, serving both rural and urban communities

> The pattern across models: start from trust and small sums, build records, and let successful borrowers climb to bigger, more individual products.

lessons.title: Understanding Microloan Pricing
lessons.content:
## Two Ways to Quote Interest

Microloans are priced in two ways that sound identical but are not. Understanding the difference is the single most important pricing skill for a borrower or a student of microfinance.

**Flat interest** is charged on the **original loan amount for the whole term**, even as you repay. Borrow $100 for 10 months at a 20% flat rate, and you owe $20 of interest about $2 of interest every month even in the final month, when you only owe $10 of principal.

**Declining-balance interest** is charged only on what you **still owe**. At a 20% declining rate, the first month's interest is computed on $100; by the last month, it is computed on about $10. The total interest cost falls sharply.

Here is the trap: a 20% **flat** rate costs nearly twice as much as a 20% **declining** rate. As a rule of thumb, a flat rate roughly corresponds to an APR of about **1.8 to 2 times** the quoted figure, because the borrower has use of the full principal for only part of the term.

## Why Microloan Rates Are High Honestly

Interest rates on microloans often look shocking next to rich-country bank loans: annualized rates of 20%, 30%, or more are common. Why?

- **Small loans, fixed costs.** Visiting villages, appraising tiny businesses, and collecting weekly installments takes similar effort whether the loan is $100 or $10,000. Spread over a $100 loan, that cost is a large percentage.
- **High delivery expense.** Rural travel, passbooks, meetings, and cash handling are labor-intensive.
- **No collateral.** Lenders price for risk they cannot secure against property.
- **Funding costs.** MFIs themselves borrow money, sometimes at commercial rates.

Context matters: a moneylender charging 10% *per month* is usually far costlier still the MFI's 30% *per year* can be the **cheapest option in town**. That does not make high rates painless, but it explains why borrowers line up.

## APR and Transparency

Because flat quotes hide the true cost, reformers pushed for **APR (annual percentage rate)** disclosure a single number capturing interest plus fees, on a declining basis, comparable across lenders. A loan advertised at "3% per month flat" may carry an APR near 60%; a borrower comparing only the quoted numbers would never know.

Transparency initiatives now encourage lenders to publish true APRs, disclose all fees up front, and train clients to ask one question: **"What is the total cost of this loan, in cash, over its whole life?"** For a $100 loan repaid over 10 months, "I repay $120 in total" is the most honest sentence in microfinance pricing.

lessons.title: Why Savings Matter Even More Than Credit
lessons.content:
## The Forgotten Half of Finance

Microfinance became famous for loans, but ask poor households what they need most and many answer: **a safe place to save**. The logic is simple. A loan is someone else's money it must be repaid, on schedule, with interest, in good weeks and bad. Savings are your own money. They wait patiently, cost nothing to hold, and are there on the day a child falls ill or a roof leaks.

## Why the Poor Need Savings More

Poor households live with **volatility**, not just scarcity:

- Income arrives in lumps a harvest, a market season while needs arrive daily
- Emergencies are frequent and uninsured: illness, funerals, crop failures
- Opportunities appear suddenly a discounted bulk purchase, a school fee deadline and vanish just as fast

Without savings, every shock becomes a crisis solved by a moneylender, a distress sale of a goat, or a skipped meal. Researchers who tracked the daily financial diaries of very poor households the study described in the book *Portfolios of the Poor* found that even families living on a couple of dollars a day **save constantly**: in cash at home, with neighbors, in rotating groups. The demand is enormous. What is missing is a **safe, convenient place** to do it. Cash under the mattress gets stolen, eroded by inflation, or most commonly spent, because money at home is money within reach of every urgent request.

## Voluntary vs Compulsory Savings

Microfinance distinguishes two kinds of deposits.

**Compulsory savings** (also called "forced" or "compensating" savings) are required as part of a loan:

- Deposited regularly alongside loan installments
- Often **locked until the loan is repaid**
- Act as a **partial guarantee** the lender holds something if the borrower defaults
- Build the saving habit automatically, a few coins at a time

**Voluntary savings** are deposits made by choice:

- Open to anyone, whether or not they borrow
- **Withdrawable on demand** (or with agreed notice)
- A signal of real trust: clients only save voluntarily with institutions they believe will still be there next year

Many early MFIs offered only compulsory savings and regulators often barred them from taking voluntary deposits at all. Experience showed that poor savers prize **access** above almost everything: a locked deposit that cannot be reached in an emergency is of limited comfort. The best programs now combine both compulsory savings tied to loans as a guarantee and discipline device, plus voluntary accounts a family can actually live on.

## A Mini-Example

**Grace**, a tailor, must deposit $2 a week into a locked account while repaying her loan that is compulsory savings. She also keeps a voluntary account where she drops coins on good days. When her sewing machine breaks mid-term, it is the voluntary account not a moneylender that pays for the repair.

lessons.title: Deposit Products and Savings Groups
lessons.content:
## Designing Deposits for Small Savers

Serving a saver who deposits 50 cents at a time is a design challenge. Products that work share a few features:

- **No minimum balance and no fees on tiny accounts** a $1 monthly fee can devour a small saver's whole balance
- **Nearby access** village agents, market-day collection, or mobile phones instead of distant branches
- **Simple records** a passbook the saver can read and trust
- **Commitment options** accounts that lock until a goal date, helping savers protect money from daily temptation and from pressure by relatives

**Mobile money** transformed this landscape: in Kenya and beyond, phone-based accounts let people deposit and withdraw at corner shops, bringing the cost of even the smallest transaction close to zero.

## ROSCAs: The Rotating Pot

Long before banks reached their villages, communities built their own institutions. A **ROSCA** rotating savings and credit association is elegantly simple:

1. A group of, say, **ten neighbors** agrees that each will contribute **$10 every month**
2. Each month, one member takes the whole **$100 pot**
3. The pot rotates until everyone has received it once; then the group may start a new round

A ROSCA turns scattered small savings into useful lump sums exactly what a school fee, a bulk purchase, or a bicycle requires. The order of receiving matters: members who need money urgently negotiate for early turns. ROSCAs need no outside lender, no paperwork, and no interest their currency is trust and the social cost of letting the group down. They exist under local names on every continent: *tontines* in West Africa, *chit funds* in India, *tandas* in Mexico.

Their limits are real: members **earn no interest**, a member might take the pot early and then stop paying, and the pot size is capped by what the group can contribute.

## VSLAs: The Community Bank in a Box

A **VSLA** village savings and loan association upgrades the ROSCA idea:

- **15 to 30 members** save together weekly, buying "shares" worth a few cents each
- The pooled fund makes **small internal loans** to members, repaid with interest the group sets itself
- A simple lockbox with three keys, held by three different members, guards the cash
- After roughly **9 to 12 months**, the fund is **shared out** each member receives their savings plus a slice of the interest earned

Because the interest stays inside the group, savers earn returns directly from their neighbors' loans. VSLAs need no outside institution at all, though NGOs often train groups in record-keeping. Millions of rural households especially women now save and borrow this way, often as their first step toward formal finance.

questions.q: Why do many poor households value savings even more than credit?
choices: Savings earn guaranteed high interest
Savings are their own money, available in an emergency without a repayment schedule
Savings are required by law
Credit is always free
questions.explain: A loan must be repaid on schedule in good weeks and bad; savings simply wait until the day they are needed.

questions.q: Compulsory savings are...
choices: Deposits required alongside a loan, often locked until the loan is repaid
Voluntary deposits withdrawable anytime
Government taxes on savings
Interest paid by the bank
questions.explain: Compulsory savings come with the loan contract regular locked deposits that also serve as a partial guarantee.

questions.q: One function of compulsory savings in a loan program is to...
choices: Pay the loan officer's salary
Replace weekly repayment meetings
Act as a partial guarantee while building the saving habit
Disqualify borrowers who own no land
questions.explain: The locked deposit gives the lender something to hold against default while teaching the borrower to save regularly.

questions.q: The key feature of voluntary savings is that...
choices: They are locked until the loan ends
They can be deposited by choice and withdrawn on demand
Only existing borrowers may hold them
They can never earn interest
questions.explain: Voluntary accounts are open to anyone and accessible when needed access is what poor savers prize most.

questions.q: The financial diaries described in *Portfolios of the Poor* found that...
choices: Poor households never save
Only wealthy households save
Even very poor households save constantly they just lack safe, convenient places to do it
Savings groups always collapse
questions.explain: Households living on a couple of dollars a day save in cash, with neighbors, and in groups the missing piece is a safe place.

questions.q: Which product feature matters most for very small savers?
choices: High minimum balances
Monthly fees on every account
Branches only in capital cities
No minimum balance, tiny or no fees, and nearby access
questions.explain: A $1 monthly fee can erase a small balance, so tiny accounts need no minimums, low fees, and close-by access points.

questions.q: In a ROSCA...
choices: Members contribute a fixed amount each round and take turns receiving the whole pot
A bank lends to the group as a whole
Members buy shares that are never returned
Only the group's leader is allowed to save
questions.explain: Ten neighbors contributing $10 a month create a $100 pot that rotates to one member each round.

questions.q: Which is a genuine limitation of ROSCAs?
choices: They require collateral
They charge high interest
Members earn no interest, and a member might take the pot early and stop paying
They require mobile phones
questions.explain: ROSCAs pay no interest and run purely on trust, so early winners can default on later rounds.

questions.q: In a VSLA, at the end of a cycle of roughly 9 to 12 months...
choices: The fund is donated to an NGO
The fund is shared out each member gets their savings plus a slice of the interest earned
The MFI takes the fund as fees
All loans convert to grants
questions.explain: The share-out returns each member's savings plus their portion of the interest the group's internal loans earned.

questions.q: In a VSLA, the interest paid on internal loans...
choices: Goes to a distant bank
Is paid to the government
Is kept by whoever guards the lockbox
Stays inside the group and is earned by the members themselves
questions.explain: Members lend their own pooled savings to each other, so the interest flows back to the savers at share-out.

lessons.title: Why Poor Households Need Insurance
lessons.content:
## The Risk Trap

Low-income households live with risk every day. A single shock a fever that requires hospital care, a flood that destroys a harvest, a fire in a market stall, the death of a breadwinner can erase years of careful saving. Because the poor have few cushions, they are forced into coping strategies that make things worse: selling a productive animal, pulling children out of school, skipping meals, or borrowing from a moneylender at crushing rates. Economists call this the **poverty ratchet**: each shock pushes the household down a rung, and the coping strategy makes climbing back harder.

> Insurance does not prevent shocks. It prevents shocks from becoming catastrophes.

## What Micro-Insurance Is

**Micro-insurance** is insurance designed for low-income people. It works on the same principle as ordinary insurance **risk pooling**. Many people each pay a small, affordable **premium** into a common pool. Only a few will suffer a loss in any given period, and the pool pays their **claims**. The amounts are scaled down: premiums may be a few cents a week, and coverage might be a few hundred dollars small for an insurer, but life-changing for a family facing a hospital bill.

To work for poor clients, micro-insurance must be:

- **Simple** one page of terms, in plain language, with no fine-print traps
- **Affordable** premiums matched to what households can actually pay
- **Accessible** sold and serviced where clients already are
- **Fast** claims paid in days, not months, because a grieving family cannot wait

## How It Works in Practice

A formal insurance company usually underwrites the product, because insurance is a regulated business. But insurers rarely reach village clients directly. Instead they partner with organizations the poor already trust microfinance institutions, cooperatives, funeral societies, or mobile phone companies. A common arrangement is a **group policy**: one contract covers all members of a cooperative or all borrowers of an MFI, which dramatically lowers administration costs per person.

Consider Amina, a market trader. She pays a small weekly premium, collected together with her loan installment, so that a hospital visit will not wipe out her savings. When her son breaks his arm, the clinic bill is covered, she keeps her stall stocked, and her daughter stays in school. That is the entire logic of micro-insurance in one story: a tiny, predictable cost replaces a huge, unpredictable one.

The pool only survives if premiums roughly match payouts plus running costs, so product design is a careful balancing act the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.title: Products, Premiums, and Delivery
lessons.content:
## The Main Products

Micro-insurance comes in a few core products, each targeting a shock that poor households fear most.

- **Life and credit-life insurance.** The most common product by far. A small life policy pays funeral costs and gives the family a modest sum. **Credit-life** covers the borrower's outstanding loan if they die or become disabled, so a widow does not inherit her husband's debt. Many MFIs bundle credit-life automatically with every loan.
- **Health insurance.** Covers clinic visits, medicines, and hospital stays. It is the product clients want most and the hardest to run well, because claims are frequent, costs vary, and fraud is tempting.
- **Crop insurance.** Pays out when drought, flood, or pests destroy a harvest. Traditional crop insurance required expensive farm-by-farm loss assessments, so a newer approach, **index insurance**, pays based on an objective trigger for example, rainfall below a set level at the local weather station. No farm visits and faster payouts, but sometimes the index fails to match a farmer's actual loss; this gap is called **basis risk**.
- **Livestock insurance.** Covers the death of animals often a family's most valuable asset. Some schemes in East Africa use satellite measures of vegetation as an index: when grazing land dries up, herders receive payouts before their animals die.

## Designing Premiums

Premiums must fit the rhythm of poor households' cash flow. A farmer earns money at harvest; a market trader earns it daily. Good products therefore collect **small, frequent payments** weekly at market day, mobile deductions, or a single premium at harvest time. Coverage is kept modest so premiums stay low. Some governments and donors subsidize premiums, especially for crop insurance, to get schemes started. But a scheme that permanently costs more than it collects will collapse, so designers walk a line between **affordability** for clients and **sustainability** for the pool.

## Delivery: Meeting Clients Where They Are

Insurers almost never sell micro-insurance directly. They rely on **delivery channels** clients already use:

- **MFIs and cooperatives** bundle insurance with loans or savings, using existing trust and payment flows. This is cheap and effective, though bundling can hide costs from clients.
- **Mobile money** lets people pay premiums by phone and receive payouts the same way a major reason micro-insurance has spread in Kenya, Tanzania, and Ghana. Mobile networks reach villages no insurance agent ever visits.
- **Community-based schemes** pool members' own contributions, common for health coverage.

Two problems haunt every scheme. First, **trust**: families who have seen a claim denied may refuse to buy again, so paying legitimate claims quickly is the best marketing. Second, **fraud and selection**: people who know they are sick are likelier to buy health cover (**adverse selection**), and insured people may take more risks (**moral hazard**). Group policies, waiting periods, and simple verification keep these in check.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of micro-insurance?
choices: To make poor households wealthy over time
To prevent small shocks from becoming financial catastrophes
To replace the need for savings entirely
To guarantee that household income grows every year
questions.explain: Micro-insurance pools risk so that one shock illness, death, crop failure does not wipe out savings or push a family deeper into poverty.

questions.q: Risk pooling means:
choices: Many people each pay a small premium into a common pool that pays the claims of the few who suffer losses
Banks pooling deposits to make bigger loans
Insurers sharing their profits with policyholders
Villagers storing food together for the lean season
questions.explain: Insurance works because the many who pay premiums but do not claim cover the losses of the few who do.

questions.q: Why do insurers usually partner with MFIs, cooperatives, or mobile phone companies to sell micro-insurance?
choices: Because the law forbids insurers from selling directly to individuals
Because partners take over all claim payments from the insurer
Because these channels already reach, and are trusted by, low-income clients
Because poor clients refuse to speak with insurance companies
questions.explain: Insurers rarely reach village clients directly, so they use organizations that already have trust, presence, and payment flows.

questions.q: What does credit-life insurance do?
choices: Pays funeral costs and a large inheritance
Builds the borrower's credit score
Insures the lender against currency changes
Pays off the borrower's outstanding loan if they die or become disabled
questions.explain: Credit-life ensures that a surviving family does not inherit the deceased borrower's debt, and it is often bundled with loans.

questions.q: Index insurance triggers payouts based on:
choices: A vote by a village committee
An objective measure such as rainfall recorded at a weather station
A farm-by-farm inspection of losses
The farmer's sworn statement of loss
questions.explain: Index products pay when an objective trigger (like low rainfall) is hit, avoiding costly individual loss assessments and speeding payouts.

questions.q: Basis risk refers to:
choices: The risk that the insurer goes bankrupt
The risk that premiums rise over time
The risk that the index payout does not match the farmer's actual loss
The risk of clients submitting fake claims
questions.explain: Because payouts follow the index rather than individual losses, a farmer can suffer a real loss while the index shows no trigger that mismatch is basis risk.

questions.q: For a farmer, premium collection is usually best timed:
choices: At harvest, when the farmer has cash
Weekly, regardless of season
Monthly by bank draft
Only when a claim is made
questions.explain: Premiums must fit cash flow; farmers earn in harvest lumps, so collecting at harvest works far better than weekly or monthly billing.

questions.q: Adverse selection means:
choices: Insurers refusing to cover farmers
Premiums being too low to cover claims
A mobile network failing during signup
People who know they are likely to claim being the most eager to buy insurance
questions.explain: When those most likely to claim (for example, people who are already sick) buy the most, the pool's costs rise schemes counter this with group policies and waiting periods.

questions.q: Why are coverage amounts in micro-insurance usually kept modest?
choices: Because regulations cap all insurance payouts
Because clients dislike larger coverage
To keep premiums affordable while keeping the pool sustainable
To discourage clients from claiming
questions.explain: Modest coverage keeps premiums within reach of poor households while ensuring the pool collects roughly what it pays out plus running costs.

questions.q: What builds trust in a micro-insurance scheme more than anything else?
choices: Aggressive advertising campaigns
Paying legitimate claims quickly
Bundling insurance with every loan
Charging higher premiums
questions.explain: Families who see claims paid promptly believe the product works; a single denied or delayed claim can poison trust in a whole community.

lessons.title: Lease or Loan? How Micro-Leasing Works
lessons.content:
## Two Ways to Finance an Asset

A tailor needs a sewing machine. She has two ways to pay for it. She can take a **loan**: receive cash, buy the machine herself, and repay the cash with interest. Or she can take a **lease**: a leasing company buys the machine, she uses it while making regular payments, and ownership is settled when the contract ends. In a loan, she owns the asset from day one and the lender holds a claim against her. In a lease, the **lessor** owns the asset throughout and the **lessee** merely rents the right to use it.

This difference sounds technical but matters enormously. Because the lessor keeps legal ownership, a lease is **self-collateralizing**: if the client stops paying, the lessor simply takes the machine back. There is no need for land titles, guarantors, or the other collateral that poor borrowers usually cannot provide.

## How Micro-Leasing Works

**Micro-leasing** applies this model to microenterprises the stalls, workshops, and tiny farms that MFIs serve. The steps are straightforward:

1. The client chooses the equipment she needs and its supplier.
2. The leasing company (often an MFI's leasing arm) buys it and becomes the legal owner.
3. The client pays a small **down payment**, then fixed lease installments over a set term often one to three years.
4. During the term the client uses, maintains, and insures the asset as the contract specifies.
5. At the end of the term, the contract settles ownership (the next lesson covers the options).

> With a loan you borrow money. With a lease you borrow the thing itself.

Payments are usually matched to the income the asset generates monthly for a tailor, seasonal for a farmer leasing a water pump. Because the lessor can repossess and resell the asset, **approval depends more on whether the equipment will generate cash than on the client's wealth or history**. This opens doors for clients with no credit record and no property.

Leasing is not free money, of course. The total of payments usually exceeds the cash price of the equipment, because the lessor charges for financing, administration, and risk. And a client who defaults loses the asset and everything she has already paid into it. Consider Bakari, who leases a motorcycle for his delivery business: the bike earns its own installments, but two missed payments and it goes back to the lessor. The next lesson looks at what kinds of equipment fit leasing, how ownership transfers, and when leasing genuinely beats credit.

lessons.title: Equipment, Ownership, and Ijara
lessons.content:
## What Gets Leased

Micro-leasing works best for **durable, productive equipment** assets that generate income, hold their value, and can be repossessed and resold if things go wrong. Typical examples:

- Sewing machines, weaving looms, and woodworking tools
- Refrigerators and milling machines for food processors
- Motorcycles, bicycles, and auto-rickshaws for transport businesses
- Water pumps, irrigation kits, and dairy equipment for farmers
- Solar systems for off-grid shops

Soft or fast-consumed goods stock, seed, fertilizer do not fit, because there is nothing to repossess. Those still require ordinary loans.

## Ownership at the End of the Term

Lease contracts differ in what happens when the last payment is made. In a **finance lease** (the usual micro-leasing form), ownership transfers to the client at term end, sometimes for a small final fee economically, it resembles buying on installments. In an **operating lease**, the lessor keeps the asset and the client simply hands it back or renews, which suits equipment that becomes obsolete quickly. Clients should always check the end-of-term clause before signing: it decides whether years of payments end in ownership or in nothing.

## Ijara: Leasing in Islamic Finance

Islamic finance prohibits **riba** interest on money so a conventional lease or loan can be religiously unacceptable to many Muslim clients. **Ijara** is the Islamic leasing contract that solves this. The financier buys the asset and leases it to the client for agreed rental payments; the financier's profit comes from rent on a real asset, not interest on cash. In **ijara wa iqtina** (lease ending in ownership), ownership transfers to the client when payments finish. Because the financier genuinely owns the asset during the term, it shares real ownership risk which is precisely what makes the contract permissible. Ijara is now a core product of Islamic microfinance from Sudan to Indonesia.

## When Leasing Beats Credit

Leasing is often the better choice when:

- The client **lacks collateral** the asset itself secures the deal
- The client has **no credit history**, because approval rests on the asset's earning power
- The equipment is **identifiable and resalable**, so repossession is practical
- The client wants **payments matched to the asset's income**, including seasonal schedules
- Religious rules make an interest-bearing loan unacceptable ijara fills the gap

Credit wins when the need is working capital, when the client already owns collateral and can get cheaper money, or when the asset is consumed rather than durable. A good provider offers both and helps the client match the tool to the job. The poorest clients, who own nothing, are often exactly the ones leasing serves best the asset is the collateral, and the work it does pays the rent.

questions.q: What is the core difference between a lease and a loan for buying equipment?
choices: Leases are always cheaper than loans
Leases never involve regular payments
In a lease the lessor owns the asset during the term; in a loan the client owns it from day one
Loans require no repayment
questions.explain: Ownership is the dividing line: a lessor keeps legal ownership and rents out use of the asset, while a lender provides cash and the client owns the purchase.

questions.q: Saying a lease is self-collateralizing means:
choices: The asset itself secures the deal, because the lessor can repossess it
The client must also pledge land
The lease requires a guarantor
The lessor takes no risk at all
questions.explain: Since the lessor owns the asset, default simply leads to repossession no land title or guarantor is needed.

questions.q: Approval for a micro-lease depends mainly on:
choices: The client's land holdings
The client's salary slips
The client's age and connections
Whether the equipment will generate enough cash to cover the installments
questions.explain: Because the asset secures the contract, the lessor's key question is whether it will earn its own payments, not the client's wealth or credit history.

questions.q: Which asset fits micro-leasing best?
choices: Fertilizer for one season
A motorcycle for a transport business
A stock of fresh vegetables
Seed for planting
questions.explain: Leasing suits durable, resalable, income-generating assets; consumed goods like seed, fertilizer, or stock cannot be repossessed.

questions.q: In a finance lease, what usually happens at the end of the term?
choices: The asset returns to the supplier
The contract always renews automatically
Ownership transfers to the client, sometimes for a small final fee
The lessor sells the asset to a third party
questions.explain: A finance lease economically resembles buying on installments: after the last payment (and any small final fee), the client owns the asset.

questions.q: An operating lease is most suitable when:
choices: The equipment becomes obsolete quickly, since the lessor keeps it
The client wants guaranteed ownership
The asset has no resale value
The client needs working capital
questions.explain: In an operating lease the client hands the asset back or renews, which fits fast-depreciating equipment the client does not want to own.

questions.q: Ijara is permissible in Islamic finance because:
choices: It charges hidden interest
It involves no profit at all
It is treated as a gift
The financier's profit comes from rent on a real asset it owns, not interest on money
questions.explain: Islamic finance prohibits riba (interest); in ijara the financier genuinely owns the asset and earns rent, sharing real ownership risk.

questions.q: Ijara wa iqtina means:
choices: A lease ending in ownership
A lease with no payments
An interest-free loan
A profit-and-loss sharing partnership
questions.explain: Ijara wa iqtina is the ijara variant in which ownership transfers to the client once payments are complete.

questions.q: Leasing tends to beat credit when:
choices: The client needs market stock
The client wants to consume the asset quickly
The client lacks collateral and needs durable, resalable equipment
The client already has access to cheap bank credit
questions.explain: Leasing shines when the client has no collateral or credit history but needs a durable asset whose income can cover the payments.

questions.q: Credit is usually a better choice than leasing for:
choices: Working capital and goods that are consumed quickly
Durable machines with resale value
Clients with no credit history
Clients who require Islamic finance
questions.explain: Loans fit needs like stock, seed, or fertilizer things that are used up rather than repossessed where leasing cannot work.

lessons.title: Budgeting an Irregular Income, Managing Debt
lessons.content:
## The Problem of Lumpy Cash Flow

A salaried worker earns the same amount every month. A poor household rarely does. A farmer's income arrives in two or three harvest lumps; a market trader's rises and falls with the season; a casual laborer simply does not know what next week brings. Meanwhile expenses food, rent, school fees, medicine arrive steadily. **Budgeting on an irregular income means bridging the gap between lumpy income and steady spending.**

The core technique is to plan around the *lean* season, not the good one:

- **Estimate a floor income** what the household earns in its worst normal month and keep essential spending inside it
- **Save aggressively in good times**, treating the surplus as the lean season's wages, not as a bonus
- **Separate the money physically**: different tins, envelopes, or mobile wallets for food, school fees, business stock, and emergencies, so one bad week cannot raid everything
- **List fixed obligations** (rent, loan installments, fees) and pay them first from any income that arrives

Financial diaries research notably the *Portfolios of the Poor* project found that poor households are already active, sophisticated money managers, juggling savings clubs, rotating groups, and small loans precisely because their incomes are unreliable. Good financial literacy training builds on those habits rather than replacing them.

## Managing Debt Wisely

Debt is a tool: used well it buys assets that raise income; used badly it eats the household alive. A few rules keep debt productive:

- **Borrow for income, not consumption**, whenever possible a loan for stock repays itself; a loan for a feast does not
- **Match the installment to cash flow**: a farmer should not carry weekly repayments due long before harvest
- **Know the real cost** ask for the total amount repayable, not just the flat rate, and compare across lenders
- **One loan at a time.** Taking a second loan to repay the first is the classic doorway into a debt spiral
- **Keep a small emergency buffer**, even one week's expenses, so a single shock cannot force a distress loan

> The question is never 'can I get the loan?' It is 'can the payments fit inside my worst month?'

Consider Mariam, a vegetable seller. Her wholesaler offers a bigger loan for festival stock; she checks her lean-month figures first, borrows only what those figures can carry, and keeps her school-fee envelope untouched. Households that master these two skills smoothing lumpy income and keeping debt productive are the same households that use microfinance safely. The next lesson looks at the other side of the contract: what lenders owe their clients.

lessons.title: Client Protection and the Over-Indebtedness Trap
lessons.content:
## What Clients Are Owed

Microfinance grew up promising to serve the poor, but serving is not the same as protecting. As the industry commercialized, scandals hidden fees, abusive collection, mass defaults forced it to define what clients are owed. The most widely used framework is the **Client Protection Principles**, developed by the global Smart Campaign. In plain terms:

1. **Appropriate products** designed for client needs, not just lender convenience
2. **Prevention of over-indebtedness** lend only what the household's cash flow can repay
3. **Transparency** full disclosure of prices, terms, and conditions in understandable language
4. **Responsible pricing** costs that are affordable and in line with the market
5. **Fair and respectful treatment** no discrimination, no abusive or coercive collection
6. **Privacy of client data** personal information protected, not sold or exposed
7. **Complaint mechanisms** a working channel for clients to raise and resolve problems

These principles matter because microfinance clients often cannot read a contract's fine print, cannot switch lenders easily, and may face social pressure from group lending. Protection is not charity; it is the lender's side of the bargain.

## Over-Indebtedness: The Warning Signs

**Over-indebtedness** means a household's debt payments have outgrown its ability to pay without serious harm. It damages clients, and it damages lenders too over-indebted clients default. Both sides should watch for the classic warning signs:

- **Borrowing to repay** a new loan taken mainly to service an old one
- **Multiple parallel loans** from several lenders at once, each invisible to the others
- **Skipping meals or selling productive assets** to make installments
- **Repayment consuming a large share of income** many practitioners treat debt service above roughly a third of household income as a danger zone
- **Hiding debts from family members**, or constant anxiety and conflict over payments
- **Dropping out of savings** the household stops saving entirely because every coin goes to creditors

> Debt distress rarely arrives suddenly. It accumulates quietly, one small top-up loan at a time.

Responsible lenders check repayment capacity before lending, share data through **credit bureaus** so parallel borrowing becomes visible, and restructure rather than punish when a good client hits a genuine shock. Clients, for their part, should treat the warning signs as an alarm bell: the moment a loan requires skipping meals or borrowing to repay, it is time to talk to the lender and to stop adding debt. Financial literacy and client protection are two halves of one idea: informed clients and responsible lenders make credit safe.

questions.q: What is the core budgeting technique for an irregular income?
choices: Spend freely in good months and hope for the best
Build essential spending around the lean-season floor income
Save only whatever is left after spending
Avoid planning because income is unpredictable
questions.explain: Planning around the worst normal month and saving good-month surpluses bridges the gap between lumpy income and steady expenses.

questions.q: Why separate money into different envelopes, tins, or mobile wallets?
choices: Because the law requires it
To hide money from lenders
To make budgeting unnecessary
So one bad week cannot raid money meant for school fees or stock
questions.explain: Physically separating money by purpose protects essentials like fees and stock from being absorbed by everyday shortfalls.

questions.q: The Portfolios of the Poor research found that poor households:
choices: Are active, sophisticated managers juggling many financial tools
Never save at all
Use only cash kept at home
Are unable to plan ahead
questions.explain: Financial diaries showed poor households actively combining savings clubs, rotating groups, and loans precisely because their incomes are unreliable.

questions.q: The first rule of wise borrowing is:
choices: Always take the largest loan offered
Borrow from several lenders at once
Borrow for income rather than consumption whenever possible
Borrow mainly for ceremonies
questions.explain: A loan that buys income-generating assets can repay itself; consumption loans must be repaid from income the household does not yet have.

questions.q: The classic doorway into a debt spiral is:
choices: Paying installments early
Taking a new loan to repay an old one
Keeping an emergency buffer
Comparing lenders before borrowing
questions.explain: Borrowing to repay means the debt itself is generating the need for more debt the signature of a spiral.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven Client Protection Principles?
choices: Transparency
Prevention of over-indebtedness
Privacy of client data
Guaranteed approval of every loan application
questions.explain: The principles cover appropriate products, transparency, responsible pricing, fair treatment, privacy, complaint mechanisms, and preventing over-indebtedness never guaranteed approval.

questions.q: The transparency principle requires lenders to provide:
choices: Full disclosure of prices, terms, and conditions in understandable language
Verbal promises only
Publication of client names
Flat-rate quotes without stating the total cost
questions.explain: Transparency means clients can see and understand the full price and terms of what they are signing before they sign it.

questions.q: Which is a warning sign of over-indebtedness?
choices: Saving regularly
One loan with affordable installments
Skipping meals or selling productive assets to make payments
Asking about the total repayable amount
questions.explain: When debt service forces a household to cut meals or sell the assets that earn its income, the debt has outgrown the ability to pay.

questions.q: Many practitioners treat debt service above what share of household income as a danger zone?
choices: About 5 percent
Roughly one third
About 10 percent
About three quarters
questions.explain: A common rule of thumb flags trouble once repayments consume more than roughly a third of household income.

questions.q: How do credit bureaus help prevent over-indebtedness?
choices: By lending directly to clients
By guaranteeing loan approval
By setting interest rates
By making parallel borrowing from multiple lenders visible
questions.explain: When lenders share data through a bureau, a client stacking loans from several sources becomes visible, so lenders can refuse to overload them.

lessons.title: The Many Shapes of an MFI
lessons.content:
## Not All MFIs Are Alike

Microfinance institution is an umbrella term covering very different organizations that share one mission: financial services for people the formal banking system ignores. The four main types differ in ownership, regulation, and what they are allowed to do especially whether they may take **deposits from the public**.

**NGO microfinance.** The original form. A non-governmental, non-profit organization lends to the poor, funded by donations, grants, and soft loans from donors. NGOs are mission-driven, reach very poor clients, and move fast but in most countries they are *not* licensed to take voluntary deposits, so they can only lend out money they raise. Grameen-style programs and countless village lending schemes began this way.

**Cooperatives and credit unions.** Owned by their **members**, who are both savers and borrowers. Members buy shares, elect the board (one member, one vote), and share surpluses. Because they pool member savings, co-ops can usually take deposits from members. They range from tiny village savings-and-credit cooperatives to large regulated credit unions. Their strength is local trust and member control; their weakness is that governance can be amateur, and poor management risks members' own savings.

**Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs).** Companies licensed to lend and sometimes to offer other services but without full banking licenses, so they generally cannot take demand deposits. NBFIs are regulated, can raise commercial investment, and often grow faster than NGOs. Many specialized microfinance companies take this legal form.

**Commercial microfinance banks.** Fully licensed banks specializing in microfinance. They can do everything: accept deposits from the public, lend, move money, and offer payment services. Deposit-taking is the prize savings from thousands of poor clients provide cheap, stable funding and give clients a safe place to save. The cost is heavy: capital requirements, supervision, reporting, and professional management.

> Same mission, different machinery: who owns the institution, who regulates it, and whether it may hold the public's savings.

## Choosing the Right Form

Each form trades reach against rigor. Consider Fatou, who saves with her village credit union, while the market town nearby is served by a regulated microfinance bank. Her co-op knows her by name and answers to its members; the bank offers her nephew a debit account and payment services the co-op cannot. NGOs reach the poorest but depend on donors. Co-ops are democratic but sometimes fragile. NBFIs scale with investor money but stay one step from full banking. Microfinance banks unlock deposits and scale at the price of regulation. The next lesson covers how institutions move along this path, and how **governance** keeps them honest.

lessons.title: Transformation and Governance
lessons.content:
## From NGO to Regulated Bank

Many of today's regulated microfinance banks began as small NGO lending projects. The journey from charity to bank is called **transformation**, and institutions make it for practical reasons:

- **Deposits.** Only a licensed institution can legally mobilize voluntary savings from the public and deposits are the cheapest, most stable funding an MFI can get, freeing it from donor cycles.
- **Scale.** A regulated shareholding company can raise equity from investors, which grants and soft loans cannot match.
- **Permanence.** Donors leave; a licensed institution can outlive any funding program.
- **Client demand.** Poor clients want savings and payments, not only loans.

Transformation is not just a paperwork change. The NGO typically creates a new regulated company, sells shares to investors (often including socially minded funds), hires professional managers, and submits to the central bank's supervision: minimum capital, reporting, audits, and inspections. The original NGO may keep a stake and continue social programs on the side.

The risks are real. New owners want financial returns, and the fear of **mission drift** gradually abandoning the poorest clients for wealthier, more profitable ones hangs over every transformation. The famous stock market listing of Mexico's Compartamos in 2007 made early investors rich while the institution charged very high interest rates, sparking a global debate about where serving the poor ends and profiting from them begins. Defenders answer that scale itself serves the poor, reaching clients no charity could.

## Governance: Keeping the Institution Honest

**Governance** is the system that directs and controls an institution who owns it, who sits on its board, and who watches the managers. Good governance in an MFI includes:

- A **board** with real skills (finance, law, the industry) and independent members, not just the founders' friends
- Clear separation between the board, which sets policy and oversees, and **management**, which runs daily operations
- Honest **financial reporting**, external audits, and supervision by the regulator
- Transparent ownership and protection of member or depositor interests
- **Double bottom line** thinking: the board explicitly tracks both financial sustainability and social mission who is reached, at what cost, with what protection

Failures of governance are behind most microfinance disasters: credit unions looted by insiders, transformed MFIs that drifted into pure profit-chasing, NGOs whose charismatic founders answered to no one. The institution's legal form matters less than whether someone with power is watching and cares about both the money and the mission.

> An MFI asks poor people to trust it with their livelihoods. Governance is how it earns that trust every year, not just at founding.

lessons.title: Reading the Loan Book: PAR30, Provisions, and Write-offs
lessons.content:
## Repayment Is Everything

Microfinance institutions (MFIs) run on thin margins and heavy trust. Because most borrowers offer no physical collateral, the single most important signal of institutional health is whether clients repay on time. The industry tracks this with a small set of standardized risk metrics that managers, funders, and regulators all watch.

## Portfolio at Risk (PAR)

**Portfolio at risk (PAR)** measures the slice of the loan book in danger. **PAR30** the most common version is the outstanding balance of all loans with at least one payment **30 or more days late**, divided by the total gross loan portfolio.

- Example: an MFI with a 10 million dollar portfolio and 400,000 dollars in loans 30+ days overdue has a PAR30 of 4 percent.
- A widely used rule of thumb: PAR30 under roughly 5 percent is considered healthy; above that, alarms should ring.
- PAR is **balance-weighted**, not head-counted. One large late loan hurts PAR more than ten tiny ones which is fair, because the money at risk is what matters.

Managers also track PAR1, PAR60, and PAR90 to watch how delinquency ages through the book.

## From Late Loans to Losses

A late loan is a warning; a loss is the bill. Two tools connect them:

- **Provisioning**: as a loan stays overdue, the MFI sets aside reserves against the likely loss. Typical policies escalate a modest provision after 30 days, larger ones at 60 and 90 days, and near-full provisioning for severely late loans. Provisions reduce profits immediately, so rising PAR quickly squeezes earnings.
- **Write-offs**: when a loan is judged uncollectible often after about 180 days of delinquency it leaves the balance sheet. The **write-off ratio** (write-offs over the average portfolio) shows realized losses.

PAR is a **leading indicator**: it predicts tomorrow's losses. Write-offs are **lagging**: they confirm yesterday's. Watch both.

## Hiding Places

Risk metrics can be gamed. **Ever-greening** restructuring a delinquent loan, or issuing a fresh one so the borrower can pay the old one makes the book look current while the underlying risk grows. Honest reporting, surprise portfolio audits, and strict restructuring rules keep the numbers real.

> A microfinance portfolio can look fine right up until it does not repayment discipline is a culture, not a number.

Good risk measurement is not bureaucracy. It protects the donor funds, savings, and future lending capacity that the next borrowers will need.

lessons.title: Liquidity, Operational Risk, and the Group-Lending Safety Net
lessons.content:
## Liquidity Risk: Short Money, Long Loans

MFIs must pay their own bills salaries, rent, and repayments to the banks and funds that finance them whether or not borrowers repay. **Liquidity risk** is the danger of running out of cash at the wrong moment.

- **Maturity mismatch**: many MFIs borrow on 12-month credit lines while issuing 18-month loans. If funders refuse to renew, lending stops mid-stream.
- **Repayment shocks**: a flood, a price crash, or even a rumor can make many borrowers stop paying at once, drying up cash inflows within weeks.
- Prudent managers hold cash buffers, diversify funding sources, and stagger funding maturities.

## Operational Risk: People, Cash, and Systems

Microfinance runs on thousands of tiny cash transactions handled in the field. That creates **operational risk** losses from failed processes, people, or systems.

- **Fraud**: a loan officer invents ghost borrowers, pockets the disbursed cash, and books fake repayments until the scheme collapses.
- **Theft and error**: physical cash moves between villages and branches; weak dual-control practices invite leakage.
- **Systems failure**: a broken management information system (MIS) can misstate balances, hide delinquency, or lose records entirely.

Standard defenses include dual custody of cash, rotating loan officers between areas, surprise audits, and separating the people who disburse money from the people who record it.

## Why Group Lending Manages Risk

Classic microfinance was invented to control credit risk without collateral. Its machinery is social:

- **Peer screening**: borrowers form their own groups often five people and members know each other's businesses and character better than any loan officer could. The unreliable get filtered out at formation.
- **Joint liability**: members guarantee one another. If one person misses a payment, the others must cover it or the whole group loses access to future loans.
- **Social collateral**: reputation replaces land titles. Defaulting means losing standing with neighbors, not just with a bank.
- **Dynamic incentives**: a clean record unlocks larger future loans, making tomorrow's credit worth more than today's default.
- **Efficiency**: groups meet together, so one officer serves many clients and spots trouble early.

The model has limits. Group pressure can shade into coercion, and because members' fortunes are linked, one local shock can trigger **collective default** the group that protects the lender in good times can collapse together in bad ones. Even so, for decades group lending kept repayment high enough to make uncollateralized lending to poor households viable the core risk insight on which the industry was built.

lessons.title: The Double Bottom Line and Measuring Social Performance
lessons.content:
## Two Bottom Lines, One Balance Sheet

Microfinance institutions (MFIs) promise something unusual: to be **financially sustainable** while also **reducing poverty**. These twin goals are called the **double bottom line**. The first bottom line is money enough revenue from interest and fees to cover costs, pay staff, and grow. The second is social reaching poor clients, especially women and rural households, and improving their lives.

The tension is real. Serving very poor, remote clients is expensive: small loans cost almost as much to administer as large ones. When funding gets tight, an MFI faces a choice push into poorer areas (the social goal) or serve better-off urban clients with bigger loans (the financial goal). Drifting toward richer clients is common enough that it has a name: **mission drift**.

## Measuring Outreach

Social performance starts with counting. Managers track:

- **Breadth of outreach** how many clients are served
- **Depth of outreach** how poor those clients are
- **Average loan size** a rough proxy for depth, since poorer borrowers usually take smaller loans

But counting clients says nothing about whether their lives improved. That requires measuring poverty itself.

## The Poverty Probability Index

The most widely used tool is the **Poverty Probability Index (PPI)** formerly the Progress out of Poverty Index developed with the Grameen Foundation and now managed by Innovations for Poverty Action. It works like this:

- A short survey of about **ten questions**, tailored to each country (roof material, cooking fuel, children in school, asset ownership)
- Answers are scored against national household survey data
- The result estimates the **likelihood** a household falls below a poverty line

> The PPI cannot prove a loan caused change, but it tells an MFI who it is actually reaching and whether that mix is shifting over time.

Mini-example: an MFI in Peru finds 40% of new clients are likely below the national poverty line, up from 28% three years earlier evidence that its rural expansion is genuinely reaching poorer households rather than drifting upward.

## The Women's Empowerment Claim

Roughly **four in five** microfinance clients worldwide are women. The industry argues that lending to women empowers them: income rises, bargaining power at home grows, children stay in school. The logic is plausible and women do tend to repay reliably, which is one reason lenders target them.

But the evidence is mixed:

- Some studies find women hand loans to **male relatives** who control the business
- Empowerment is hard to measure; household income can rise while a woman's control does not
- Group meetings, training, and savings habits may matter as much as the loan itself

Honest practitioners now treat empowerment as a **goal to verify**, not a slogan to assume.

## Social Performance Management

Industry bodies such as the **Social Performance Task Force** have written universal standards: define a social mission, measure it, report it, and act on the findings. The lesson of a decade of measurement is simple what gets measured gets managed, and what gets assumed gets exaggerated.

lessons.title: What the Evidence Says and the Critics
lessons.content:
## The Randomized Revolution

For years, microfinance impact claims rested on **before-and-after stories**: a borrower took a loan, her business grew, therefore microfinance works. The problem is **selection** people who choose to borrow may be more entrepreneurial to begin with, so they might have prospered anyway. In the 2000s, researchers including **Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo** began running **randomized controlled trials (RCTs)**: some communities received microfinance access while similar communities did not, and outcomes were compared.

Around 2015, six such studies conducted in India (Hyderabad), Morocco, Mexico, Mongolia, Bosnia, and Ethiopia were published together, mostly in the *American Economic Journal: Applied Economics*. For the first time, the sector had rigorous, comparable evidence.

## What the Studies Found

The headline results were sobering but not hopeless:

- **No average transformation** households with microcredit access did not, on average, earn or consume dramatically more
- **Real but modest business effects** some existing businesses expanded, and a slice of more entrepreneurial households benefited noticeably
- **Little movement on schooling or health** children were not clearly more likely to stay in school
- **Greater financial freedom** households shifted spending, cut temptation goods, and gained flexibility to manage ups and downs

A typical pattern: a tailor in Hyderabad uses a loan to buy a second sewing machine, works longer hours, and earns more while her neighbor simply replaces expensive informal debt with a cheaper microfinance loan. Both are better off; neither escapes poverty.

## The Critics' Case

Critics argue the sector oversold itself:

- **Interest rates are high** often roughly 25-40% a year or more, a heavy burden for the poor
- **Over-indebtedness** easy access plus group pressure can trap borrowers in cycles of re-borrowing
- **Collection pressure** weekly meetings and joint liability can turn coercive
- **Opportunity cost** the money might do more good in savings, insurance, or job-creation programs

Some development thinkers go further, calling microcredit a distraction from the bigger drivers of poverty: jobs, infrastructure, and health.

## The Middle Ground

The fairest reading of the evidence: microfinance is a **useful tool, not a miracle**. It helps poor households manage money, smooth consumption, and sometimes grow tiny businesses genuinely valuable outcomes but it does not, on its own, lift whole communities out of poverty.

## Why the Findings Matter

The RCT results changed practice. Donors shifted attention toward **savings, payments, and insurance**; MFIs added flexible products and financial training; marketers stopped promising miracles. Credible impact claims now sound like the evidence: *modest, real, and uneven* which is exactly what honest social performance reporting should say.

lessons.title: Mobile Money and the Digital Rails
lessons.content:
## From Cash to Keypads

Traditional microfinance ran on **cash**: loan officers carried money to villages, borrowers repaid at weekly meetings, and every note was counted by hand. That changed when **mobile money** arrived most famously **M-Pesa**, launched in Kenya in 2007 by Safaricom. Mobile money lets people store value on a phone account and send it by simple text commands no bank account or smartphone required.

Within a few years, tens of millions of Kenyans were using it, and the model spread across East Africa, South Asia, and beyond. For microfinance, it was the missing infrastructure: **rails** on which cheaper, faster financial services could run.

## How Agent Networks Work

Mobile money is not pure software; it depends on **agents** small shopkeepers who convert between cash and electronic value:

- A customer hands the agent **cash**, and the agent credits her phone wallet (a *cash-in*)
- To withdraw, the customer sends e-money to the agent, who hands over **cash** (a *cash-out*)
- Agents manage their **float** the balance of e-money and physical cash they hold and earn commissions on each transaction

Mini-example: a farmer sells maize, receives payment on her phone, and walks to the corner kiosk to cash out part of it for market day. The kiosk owner is the human face of the digital system. Without a dense agent network, digital money is just numbers on a screen.

## Why Mobile Money Matters for Microfinance

The rails cut costs at every step:

- **Disbursement** loans arrive instantly on a phone instead of at a weekly meeting
- **Repayment** borrowers pay from home instead of traveling to a branch
- **Records** every transaction creates a **digital trail** that institutions can analyze
- **Savings** even tiny balances can be held safely without a bank branch

Lower cost per transaction makes smaller loans viable, so the economics of serving the very poor improve.

## Digital Credit Scoring

The biggest change is invisible: **data**. Poor borrowers historically had no credit history, so lending to them was a gamble. Digital systems create substitutes:

- **Mobile money history** steady flows in and out suggest income stability
- **Airtime top-ups** frequent, consistent purchases signal cash management
- **Bill payments and remittances** evidence of obligations met
- **Psychometric tests** short quizzes measuring traits like planning and honesty, used by lenders such as EFL

Algorithms combine these signals into a **credit score** for someone a traditional bank could not assess at all.

## The Invisible Become Visible

A shopkeeper with no payslip, no collateral, and no bank statement can now be scored in minutes. That is the genuine promise of digital microfinance not replacing the loan officer's judgment everywhere, but extending a first rung of the financial ladder to people the old system could never reach profitably.

lessons.title: Instant Nano-Loans: Opportunity and Risk
lessons.content:
## Credit in Ninety Seconds

Digital rails plus automated scoring produced something new: the **nano-loan** a tiny, instant, short-term loan delivered entirely by phone. A typical offer: **$20 for two weeks**, approved in minutes, with no paperwork, no meeting, and no collateral. Apps and mobile-money menus across Africa and South Asia now push such offers to millions of people.

The borrower experience is radically simple:

- Open the menu or app and request an amount
- An algorithm scores you instantly from your phone and transaction data
- Money lands in your wallet; repayment is due on a set date

For a market vendor who needs stock before dawn, this is transformative compared with a two-week group-lending process.

## The Opportunities

- **Emergency smoothing** a small loan can bridge a medical bill or a slow sales week without selling assets
- **Credit histories** repaid nano-loans create records that can unlock larger, cheaper credit later
- **Competition** new digital lenders pressure traditional MFIs to cut costs and speed up
- **Convenience** no travel, no waiting, no lost work hours

## Risk One: Privacy

Speed comes from **data extraction**, and some lenders go too far:

- Apps request access to **contact lists, messages, photos, and location**
- Collection tactics have included **debt-shaming** messaging a borrower's friends and family about missed payments
- Consent is often meaningless: declining permissions means declining the loan

Your phone becomes the collateral and the pressure device.

## Risk Two: Algorithmic Bias

Automated scoring is **opaque**:

- Nobody explains why you were denied or offered a smaller limit
- Models trained on biased data can **systematically disadvantage** women, rural users, or particular groups even without intending to
- Errors are hard to appeal when there is no loan officer to ask

> A score that no one can explain is a verdict that no one can challenge.

## Risk Three: Digital Over-Indebtedness

The features that make nano-loans attractive also make them dangerous:

- **Frictionless re-borrowing** repay today, borrow again tonight
- **Multiple apps** borrowers stack loans across lenders who cannot see each other
- **Fee structures** small fees on very short terms annualize to extremely high effective rates
- **Thin files** new borrowers are scored on little data, so limits can jump faster than incomes

## What Good Looks Like

Responsible digital lending needs **consumer protection fit for phones**: clear disclosure of the total cost, genuine data consent, limits on contact-list abuse, reporting to credit bureaus so lenders can see each other's loans, and a human route for complaints. The technology is neutral; the rules around it decide whether nano-loans become a ladder or a trap.
